extracted.intended_audience: poets, novelists, literary critics, and attentive readers of Romantic-era literature
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance for writing and judging Romantic-era poetry and narrative, extracted from Lamb's letters: what pleases or offends a sensitive reader (verisimilitude, simplicity, emotional effect, didacticism, meter, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didactic sign-posting
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructions conveyed in a poem or tale should not be too direct — an intelligent reader finds a sort of insult in being told, 'I will teach you how to think upon this subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipatterns: Sterne and many modern novelists who continually 'put a sign-post up to show where you are to feel' with phrases like 'Let not my reader suppose' or 'Imagine, if you can.' Good practice: let feeling 'slide into the mind of the reader' without explicit instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust the reader's intelligence (the unwritten compact)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an implied, unwritten compact between author and reader: 'I will tell you a story, and I suppose you will understand it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of the compact working well: 'Robinson Crusoe,' 'The Vicar of Wakefield,' 'Roderick Random' — 'beautiful, bare narratives' that present events without over-explanation. Avoid assuming readers are 'stupid' by over-directing their emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve verisimilitude in titling and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: A title or framing device that undercuts the tale's claim to truth (e.g., calling the 'Ancient Mariner' a 'Poet's Reverie') weakens the reader's confidence and the story's force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: titles that announce a distance or self-consciousness which makes the reader skeptical. Good practice: choose titles/frames that maintain the story's credibility and the reader's immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive characterization when the effect requires universality
rubrics_metrics.description: In tales of overwhelming, dream-like experience (as in the 'Ancient Mariner'), excessive particulars of character or profession can lessen the universality of the experience: 'the Ancient Mariner undergoes such trials as overwhelm and bury all individuality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the narrative aims to evoke a state that swallows individuality (like a bad dream), resist anchoring the protagonist with detailed backstory or social roles that distract from the elemental effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity must be genuine, not a cover for poverty
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity of expression can be admirable, but sometimes 'simplicity' is only a disguise for poverty of thought or expression: 'you sometimes doubt if simplicity be not a cover for poverty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that pared-down language still carries substantial thought and feeling. Antipattern: artful aiming at simplicity that empties the piece of richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional immediacy and power (make the reader laugh or cry)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful poem or piece should often produce an immediate emotional response — Lamb laments that the second volume 'does not often make you laugh or cry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer pieces that move the reader; Lamb cites the 'Ancient Mariner,' 'The Mad Mother,' and 'Lines at Tintern Abbey' as examples of highly affecting work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse satire or inappropriate epithets that disfigure tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Coarse or commonplace sarcasm and coarse epithets can disfigure otherwise good poems (e.g., Lamb finds the 'Poet's Epitaph' disfigured by 'common satire upon parsons and lawyers' and the coarse epithet 'pin-point').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain tonal appropriateness; harsh or low jests can harm the dignity or subtlety of a piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness can be a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Short pieces can be 'choice and genuine' — brevity often helps concentration of effect ('The best piece in it I will send you, being short').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider economy: a short, well-wrought piece may have more impact than a longer, diffuse one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary prefatory apology or authorial prose that weakens the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose apologies or explanatory prefatory remarks (e.g., Coleridge's 'prose apology, to open the eyes of dead men') can be unnecessary and may lessen the power of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the work speak for itself; avoid framing that attempts to justify or anticipate objections in a way that undermines the reading experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve wonder in children's literature; avoid turning tales into dry facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's books that present 'knowledge' in the shape of knowledge (e.g., telling a child 'a horse is an animal') displace the 'beautiful interest in wild tales which made the child a man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor stories that kindle imagination and wonder over didactic, fact-heavy presentations that blunt curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance caution: an author reading his own work may limit its effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet reads his own verses aloud he may 'have but a limited power over you' — authorial reading can expose weaknesses and limit the audience's response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful when performing your own pieces; the intimate authority of a written line can change under self-reading, and comic or awkward moments may be amplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match meter and form to the poem's character; avoid ponderous imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Meter influences pacing and effect: Chapman (long fourteen-syllable lines) 'gallops' with continuous interest, while Cowper's 'ponderous blank verse detains you every step with some heavy Miltonism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose line-length and metrical rhythm to suit the poem's energy; avoid slavish imitation of a heavy model when a lighter or more driving line better serves the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's self-awareness: critics may validly respond to parts rather than whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Lamb confesses he can 'vehemently applaud, or perversely stickle, at parts; but I cannot grasp at a whole' — critics should recognize the partial, fragmentary nature of some responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing, be explicit about whether your judgments concern isolated passages or the entire work; avoid presenting fragmentary impressions as comprehensive assessments.
